title: Does eating your evening meal earlier improve blood sugar control in adults with obesity, without changing bedtime?
official: A randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of finishing eating at least three hours before habitual bedtime, compared with usual eating patterns, on glucose control in adults with obesity who habitually eat late (the Supper Until Next Sunrise Eating Trial, SUNSET)
summary:
Background and study aims
Obesity is linked to poor blood sugar control. This increases the risk of health problems such as type 2 diabetes. Many people with obesity eat close to bedtime. It isn't clear whether this timing itself affects blood sugar, or whether it's down to differences in people's natural sleep patterns. This study will test whether finishing eating at least 3 hours before bedtime improves blood sugar levels. This will be compared with eating closer to bedtime as usual. Bedtime itself will stay the same for everyone.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 and over with obesity (a BMI of 30 or above) can take part. Participants must usually eat their last meal less than 3 hours before bed on most days of the week. They need a stable sleep schedule and their own smartphone. People with diabetes cannot take part. Nor can those with an eating disorder, who work night shifts, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or take certain medications (including weight-loss injections such as Ozempic or Wegovy).

What does the study involve?
Participants first attend a visit at the University of Plymouth. Their height, weight, and waist size are measured. They are fitted with a small glucose sensor and an activity monitor, which also tracks sleep. These are worn for 10 days. Participants also complete a short questionnaire about their sleep habits. After this, participants are put by chance into one of two groups. One group finishes eating at least 3 hours before their usual bedtime for 8 weeks. The other group eats as they normally would. Both groups keep their usual bedtime throughout. During these 8 weeks, participants log only their last meal or snack each evening, using a smartphone app. They receive brief weekly text check-ins. They also have phone or video calls with the research team at weeks 1, 4, and 8. At the end of the 8 weeks, participants wear the glucose and activity monitors again for a further 10 days. They log their full food intake on 4 of those days, and just their last meal or snack on the remaining 6. Participants then attend a final visit. Their weight and waist size are measured again, and the monitors are removed. They receive a summary of their glucose and activity results, and a shopping voucher to thank them for their time.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Taking part involves minimal risk. Some participants may feel hungry in the evening. There may be mild discomfort from wearing the glucose sensor or activity monitor. Participants receive a free health check. This includes continuous glucose monitoring and sleep and activity monitoring. At the end of the study, participants receive a written summary of their own glucose, sleep, and activity results, in plain language. The glucose data given to participants is for research purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis. Participants should not change their healthcare or medication because of this data, without first speaking to their doctor. Participants in the intervention group may see an improvement in their blood glucose control. However, this is not yet known. There is no guarantee that taking part will improve a participant's health or blood glucose control. This is the reason for the study. It is possible the intervention will have no effect, or only a small effect. Participants in the control group continue their usual eating pattern during the study. If the intervention is later found to be helpful, they will be given information about it after the study ends. Taking part contributes to research that may help guide future advice on eating timing and type 2 diabetes prevention. Participants also receive a shopping voucher at the end of the study, to thank them for their time.

Where is the study run from?
University of Plymouth (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to May 2027.

Who is funding the study?
This study is self-funded by the researcher, as part of a PhD.

interventions.name:
Participants who meet the eligibility criteria complete a 10-day baseline assessment, during which they wear a continuous glucose monitor (Dexcom ONE+) and a wrist actigraph (ActiGraph wGT3X-BT), and complete the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ) to assess chronotype.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Age ≥18 years
2.	BMI ≥30 kg/m² (obese)
3.	Very late eaters: last meal <3 hours before bed on ≥5 days/week
4.	Typically finish eating after 20:00
5.	Stable sleep schedule (bedtime variation ± 30 minutes)
6.	Own smartphone (iOS/Android) compatible with Libro Nutritics app
7.	Willing to maintain habitual sleep timing throughout study
Exclusion criteria:
1. Type 1 or 2 diabetes (self-reported or physician-diagnosed)
2. Taking medications known to impact glucose levels (e.g., corticosteroids, metformin, liraglutide, semaglutide)
3. Currently taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist medication (e.g., Ozempic, Wegovy, Saxenda, Mounjaro, Trulicity)
4. Diagnosed eating disorder
5. Shift workers or overnight workers
6. Pregnancy or lactation
7. Current participation in weight loss program
8. Health issues that might limit participation or compliance
